description: We are Team "The Orbital Five", connecting space technology with sustainable agriculture! Through NASA's Field Shift Challenge, we studied satellite data to create an intelligent crop rotation platform. Our solution offers four planning approaches: conventional rotation, water conservation, soil health optimization, and personalized farming. By turning NASA Earth observations into clear recommendations, we help farmers save water, protect soil, and build a resilient future.
summary: Field Shift is a free, bilingual (English/Persian) decision-support web app that helps farmers compare crop-rotation strategies for their own field. The farmer draws the field on a satellite map; the app then gathers 20 years of NASA POWER climate and soil-wetness data, soil properties (ISRIC SoilGrids, FAO HWSD), elevation and slope (Copernicus DEM) and FAO GAEZ crop suitability, and compares four strategies — current practice, water saving, soil health and a balance of the farmer's own priorities — with the evidence, risks and assumptions behind each. What makes it different: our team went into the field and measured soil moisture with a digital meter; the satellite values differed by about ±17 %, so the app shows satellite moisture with that uncertainty and corrects it with field points. It supports, and does not replace, the farmer's judgment.
details:
Field Shift turns open Earth-observation data into rotation choices a farmer can understand. In step 1 the farmer finds the village (in English or Persian) and draws the field on a satellite map. An automatic scan then collects seven datasets for that exact place in 1–3 minutes: place name, elevation and slope, soil texture/pH/salinity/drainage, 250 m soil properties and available water, 20 years of daily NASA POWER climate, the last 120 days of NASA POWER surface and root-zone soil wetness, and FAO GAEZ suitability for 18 crops. Short, optional questions add the farmer's crop history, water supply and priorities.

A transparent, deterministic rules engine builds four rotation strategies over the planning horizon: A — the farmer's current practice; B — water saving; C — soil health and diversity (legumes, deep roots, residue); D — balanced by the farmer's own weights. For every crop it computes FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration and a dekadal soil-water balance, the irrigation need in mm and in m³ for the field, heat and frost risk around flowering, salinity tolerance and months without water. Each strategy has a score, a data-completeness value, a crop calendar and an explanation of its advantages, disadvantages, evidence and assumptions. The farmer can replace any crop and see the effect, compare strategies side by side, and export a printable report, JSON, CSV or GeoJSON.NASA POWER soil wetness (MERRA-2, about 50 km) does not see irrigation. Our team measured surface soil moisture with a digital meter at about 10 points and found a difference of about ±17 % from the satellite. The app converts wetness to volumetric water content with SoilGrids porosity and shows it with a ±17 % uncertainty band. When field points are entered, it computes bias, MAPE, RMSE, ubRMSE (against the 0.04 m³/m³ SMAP target), correlation and a correction chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation, following Gruber et al. (2020). This answers the challenge's request to clarify how satellite observations differ from ground measurements and how combining both improves accuracy.

Field Shift uses explainable methods where farmers need to trust the result: a transparent rules engine for the strategies, statistical correction with cross-validation and an explicit uncertainty band for soil moisture, and data from different resolutions (NASA POWER ~50 km, GAEZ ~9 km, HWSD ~1 km, SoilGrids 250 m, DEM 90 m) combined for one field. An SI model is used only in the optional photo damage check, and every result reminds the user where local expertise is needed.

A farmer can photograph damaged plants. An SI model (Claude, with the user's own API key) suggests likely causes with confidence and evidence, using the last 30 days of NASA POWER weather for the field, and one click adds the host crops of soil-borne problems to the rotation's excluded crops. It is clearly labelled as a suggestion that needs expert confirmation.

Farmers see water use and risks before they plant, in their own language (Persian, right-to-left, or English), on a phone or a computer, with no installation, account or cost. All data stay in the user's browser, and every number shows its source.

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (a single-file web app, nothing to install); Leaflet and Leaflet-Geoman (maps), Chart.js, Turf.js and geotiff.js; Python build and translation tools; Node.js test suites (engine checks including FAO-56 example 18, both languages, XSS escaping, map search and phone layouts in headless Edge).

A tool that extension workers and farmers in water-stressed regions such as the Qazvin plain can use to plan rotations that save water and rebuild soil, validated against measurements in their own fields.
